subject: biology
title: Sampling and estimating populations
key_idea: Ecologists cannot count every organism, so they sample. Random sampling with quadrats and transects estimates the distribution and abundance of plants and slow-moving animals. Mark-release-recapture estimates the size of a population of motile animals using the Lincoln index.

blocks.text: Sampling measures the biodiversity of a habitat without counting every organism. A sample must be large enough and unbiased to represent the whole area.

items: **Random sampling** gives every part of the area an equal chance of being chosen. It avoids bias.
To sample randomly, divide the area into a grid and use random numbers as coordinates.
**Non-random sampling** is used when the area is not uniform. It includes opportunistic, stratified and systematic methods.
Sample the full range of organisms in a habitat, not only the most obvious ones.
A larger sample, and more samples, make the estimate more reliable.
Sampling estimates biodiversity and population size without counting everything.
Random sampling avoids bias, and a larger sample is more reliable.

blocks.text: Quadrats and transects measure the distribution and abundance of plants and slow-moving or non-motile animals.

items.meaning: How many individuals of a species there are in an area.
Where in the habitat a species is found.
A square frame of known area placed on the ground to count or estimate the organisms inside.
A line or belt laid across a habitat along which samples are taken.

items: Place quadrats at random positions using random coordinates.
Count the number of individuals, or estimate percentage cover for species that are hard to count.
Repeat many times, then calculate the mean per quadrat.
Estimate the population as the mean number per quadrat multiplied by the total area divided by the area of one quadrat.
Use a transect when conditions change gradually, for example up a shore or away from a path.
A **line transect** records the organisms touching a tape measure laid across the habitat.
A **belt transect** is a strip of a set width, normally sampled with a quadrat moved along the line.
Sample at regular intervals (systematic sampling) to show how distribution changes with an abiotic factor.
Random quadrats estimate abundance; transects show how distribution changes across a gradient.
Belt transects use quadrats along a line, so they give more detail than a line alone.

blocks.text: Motile animals move away, so quadrats do not work. Mark-release-recapture estimates their population size.

items.text: Catch a sample of animals and count them (n₁).
Mark each one in a harmless way, for example with a dot of paint.
Release them and allow time for them to mix back into the population.
Catch a second sample (n₂) and count how many are marked (m).

blocks.label: Lincoln index (estimated population size)
where: n₁ = number caught and marked in the first sample
n₂ = total number caught in the second sample
m = number of marked animals in the second sample

diagram.alt: Calculate a population size using the Lincoln index.
diagram.question: In a first sample, {n1} animals are caught and marked. In a second sample, {n2} animals are caught and {m} of them are marked. Estimate the population size.

blocks.text: The method only works if these assumptions are true.

items: The marked animals have mixed evenly back into the population.
The marking does not harm the animals or make them easier for predators to see.
The mark does not rub off or fade during the investigation.
There is no significant migration, births or deaths between the two samples.
Marked and unmarked animals are equally likely to be recaptured.
Estimated population = (first sample × second sample) ÷ marked animals recaptured.
The estimate is reliable only if the assumptions hold.

blocks.text: Different animals need different tools. Match the method to the organism and the habitat.

rows: Insects and other small animals in long grass or foliage
Small animals that walk on the ground, such as beetles
Small insects, sucked gently into a tube from a surface
Plants and slow-moving or non-motile animals

items: Pick a technique that suits the organism: nets, traps and pooters for small animals, quadrats for plants.
Whatever the method, sample randomly and repeat to make the results reliable.

checks.q: Explain why quadrats are placed at random when estimating the abundance of a plant species.
checks.a: To avoid bias, so that every part of the area has an equal chance of being sampled and the sample is representative of the whole area.

checks.q: A student marks 40 beetles. A second sample contains 30 beetles, of which 6 are marked. Calculate the estimated population.
State three assumptions made when using mark-release-recapture.
checks.a: Any three from: marked individuals mix evenly with the rest; marking does not harm or affect survival; the mark does not fade or rub off; no births, deaths or migration between samples; marked and unmarked equally likely to be caught.

items: Use randomly placed quadrats, or quadrats along a belt transect, for slow-moving or non-motile organisms.
Use mark-release-recapture for motile organisms, and know the assumptions made.
Calculate a population size from given mark-release-recapture data.
Explain why random sampling matters in measuring the biodiversity of an area.
Use frame quadrats, line transects, belt transects and mark-release-recapture with the Lincoln index.
The Lincoln index formula is given in the exam, so concentrate on using it.
Know random and non-random sampling: opportunistic, stratified and systematic.
**Opportunistic** sampling uses whatever is convenient. **Stratified** sampling samples each distinct area in proportion to its size. **Systematic** sampling takes samples at regular intervals.
Techniques to know: quadrats, sweep nets, pitfall traps and pooters.
Use sampling and recording methods to determine the distribution and abundance of organisms in a variety of ecosystems.
